lesson.title: Kalender II: Juni bis Oktober
lesson.subtitle: the second half of the Latin year — and the Roman numbers hiding inside it

hook.title: A Calendar Forgetting Its Own Numbers
hook.content: Last lesson: five Latin names that never left. These five tell a second story — a calendar slowly forgetting how to count. September is Latin septem, 'seven', and Oktober is octo, 'eight': in the old Roman year that began in March, they really were months seven and eight. Juli and August once counted too — Quintilis, 'fifth', and Sextilis, 'sixth' — until the big names moved in: Julius Caesar took the fifth month (Juli), Augustus took the sixth (August, 'the venerable one'), and Juni belongs to Juno, queen of the gods. English kept every one of these names whole — June, July, August — so this is not vocabulary, it is pronunciation: German hammers the stress onto the FIRST syllable (JU-ni, AU-gust, SEP-tem-ber) where English lets it drift (ju-LY, au-GUST, sep-TEM-ber). And the law from Kalender I still holds: months are masculine and stand bare after im — im Juni, im Oktober.

footnotes.title: The J That Isn't a J
footnotes.content: Latin's I was a Y-sound, and German still says it that way: Juni sounds like 'YOO-nee' and Juli like 'YOO-lee'. English hardened the sound into J (June, July). Same Latin name, two consonants — but the vowel never moved, which is why the months feel so familiar when you say them the German way.

pattern.title: Dates in the Second Half
pattern.content: Same three frames as Kalender I, new names. 1. With a preposition: im Juni, im Juli, im August, im September, im Oktober — 'im' is in + dem, and dem is the masculine, so the bare name follows. 2. As a subject: Der August ist heiß. 3. Weather small talk: Im Oktober regnet es oft. The arithmetic scales up: von Januar bis Oktober sind es zehn Monate. And the date frame from last lesson still works: am 5. Mai, am 1. September — ordinal, dot, bare name.
pattern.linguist_note: English pulled the stress rightward over the centuries (ju-LY, au-GUST, sep-TEM-ber, oc-TO-ber); German's first-syllable law never moved (JU-li, AU-gust, SEP-tem-ber, OK-to-ber). Two thousand years of Latin company, and German still gives every borrowed name the same German beat.

exercises.prompt: The second half of the year — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: In September it rains on four days
matching_pairs.german: Im September regnet es an vier Tagen

matching_pairs.english: From January to October there are ten months
matching_pairs.german: Von Januar bis Oktober sind es zehn Monate

exercises.target_answer: Der Juni ist warm, Im Juli schwimmen wir oft, Der August ist heiß, Im September regnet es an vier Tagen, Im Oktober fallen die Blätter, Von Januar bis Oktober sind es zehn Monate
exercises.meaning: the five months in sentences, plus the count
exercises.explanation: im + the bare masculine name, exactly as in Kalender I. And the count still runs underneath: from Januar to Oktober there are zehn Monate — the Roman count you will close out next lesson.

exercises.prompt: Which month is Latin septem — 'seven' — even though it is the ninth month of our year?
exercises.meaning: September hides the Roman number seven
exercises.explanation: The old Roman year began in March, so September really was the seventh month (septem) and Oktober the eighth (octo). When January moved to the front, the names kept their old numbers — a fossil count you now own in two languages.

exercises.prompt: The eighth month of the German calendar ('der achte Monat', after Julius Caesar's July) carries Emperor Octavian's title 'the venerable one'. Which English month is it?
exercises.meaning: August ↔ August: one emperor, one name, two languages
exercises.explanation: Augustus renamed the sixth month (Sextilis) after himself, and both German and English kept it letter for letter — only the stress moved: German AU-gust, English au-GUST. Juni keeps a goddess (Juno) and Juli an emperor (Julius Caesar) the same way.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the October sentence: 'In October the leaves fall'
exercises.explanation: Time phrase first, verb second, subject last — the German order you have been assembling all along. Fallen is the same strong verb as English fall; die Blätter is the umlauted plural of das Blatt.
habe in slot 2, the time phrase up front. Swap the month and the sentence still works: Im Juli habe ich Urlaub. The frame is yours; the calendar just fills the gap.

summary.outcome: Name Juni through Oktober, keep the first-syllable stress, and read the Roman count hiding in September and Oktober.

use_example.german: Im August ist es heiß — im Oktober fallen die Blätter.
use_example.english: In August it is hot — in October the leaves fall.

summary.takeaway: Der Juni, der Juli, der August, der September, der Oktober — masculine, bare after im, stressed on the first syllable, with septem and octo still counting inside.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: November and Dezember — the count finally closes, and the holiday words walk in with it.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Kalender II: Juni bis Oktober (In June I have vacation):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Im Juni habe ich Urlaub" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Kalender II: Juni bis Oktober without relying on short-term echo.

juni.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Iūnius. [wiktionary]

juli.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Iūlius. [wiktionary]

august.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both English and German borrowed (via French): Latin Augustus. [wiktionary]

september.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin September, inherited via Middle High German. [wiktionary]

oktober.etymology_derivation: Latin loan both languages share: Latin Octōber, from octō 'eight' — the eighth month of the old Roman calendar. [wiktionary]

monat.etymology_derivation: The twin of English month, from *mānōþ 'moon' (see der Mond) — th→d included. [wiktionary]

jahr.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *jār — the twin of English year. [wiktionary]

warm.etymology_derivation: Identical form and meaning as English warm since Old High German. [wiktionary]

regnen.context_translation: It is raining in Berlin today.
regnen.etymology_derivation: Denominal verb from Regen (rain, already known — the y→g twin of English rain). [wiktionary]

vier.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *feuwar — the direct twin of English four. [wiktionary]

zehn.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *tehun — the twin of English ten with the classic t → z shift. [wiktionary]

oft.context_translation: We often play in the park.
oft.etymology_derivation: Old High German ofta — the true twin of English oft/often. [wiktionary]

käfer.context_phrase: Ein kleiner Käfer krabbelt auf dem Blatt.
käfer.context_translation: A little beetle crawls on the leaf.
käfer.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German këvere, from Proto-West Germanic *kefrō. English chafer, as in cockchafer, is the listed cognate. [wiktionary]

rentner.context_phrase: Der Rentner geht jeden Tag spazieren.
rentner.context_translation: The pensioner goes for a walk every day.
rentner.etymology_derivation: Rente (pension) + -ner; Rente is borrowed from Old French rente, from Medieval Latin rendita - the same source as English rent. [wiktionary][etymonline]

vorfreude.context_phrase: Die Vorfreude auf den Urlaub ist groß.
vorfreude.context_translation: The anticipation of the holiday is great.
vorfreude.etymology_derivation: vor- + Freude, literally before-joy — the joy of looking forward; vor is the documented twin of fore, and Freude is the dictionary's joy-word. [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
